sla_name: Searching for information: Familiarise with various types of search engines
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to familiarise with various types of search engines accurately and confidently.
sla_teaching_aids: Computers/smartphones with internet access|Projector|Sample search results
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson introduces students to using ICT tools to familiarise with various types of search engines. Effective information search skills allow a learner to locate reliable material quickly for study and lifelong learning.
sla_notes_details: Students learn the difference between general search engines and specialised ones (e.g., Google, Google Scholar), and practise typing focused keywords instead of full sentences. They also learn to judge the reliability of a source by checking its author, date and domain, and to save or bookmark useful materials such as books, journals and articles for later use.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student researching 'causes of deforestation in Tanzania' types the keywords 'deforestation causes Tanzania' into a search engine, then compares results from a news site and an educational site to see which gives more reliable information.
sla_notes_daily_life: Learners use these same search skills at home or in a cyber cafe to complete homework, prepare presentations, or find information for personal projects.
sla_exercise: Name two examples of search engines that can be used to find information.::Any two of: Google, Google Scholar, Bing.||Why is it important to check the source of information found online?::To make sure the information is accurate and reliable before using it.||Give one keyword phrase you would type to search for information about climate change.::Any reasonable focused phrase, e.g. 'causes of climate change'.

sla_name: Listening task: Answer questions based on information from presentations/tasks
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to answer questions based on information from presentations/tasks accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to answer questions based on information from presentations/tasks after listening to spoken texts such as presentations, stories or recordings. Strong listening comprehension is the foundation for accurate spoken and written responses.
sla_notes_details: Students listen attentively to an oral text (a presentation, recording, or teacher narration), note down key words and ideas, and then use these notes to respond, summarise or paraphrase what they heard. Emphasis is placed on listening for gist first, then for specific details, before producing an accurate spoken or written response.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after listening to a short recorded story about a market day, students identify who the characters are, what happened first, next and last, and then retell the story in their own words to a partner.
sla_notes_daily_life: This skill helps learners follow announcements, instructions and conversations correctly in everyday situations such as at school, at home or on the radio.
sla_exercise: What should a listener do before trying to answer questions about a spoken text?::Listen attentively for the overall meaning (gist) before focusing on specific details.||Why is note-taking useful while listening?::It helps the listener remember key ideas to use when responding or summarising.||State one way to check that you understood a spoken message correctly.::Restate or paraphrase the message back to the speaker to confirm understanding.

specific_competence_name: Develop listening skills

sla_name: Pronunciation practice: Practise pronunciation of words from oral and audio/audio-visual s
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to practise pronunciation of words from oral and audio/audio-visual sources accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson focuses on helping students to practise pronunciation of words from oral and audio/audio-visual sources, building intelligible pronunciation and fluency in spoken English.
sla_notes_details: Students listen to a model (teacher or recording) pronouncing target words or sounds correctly, then practise through repetition, tongue twisters, games or dictation. Attention is paid to sound distinctions (minimal pairs), word stress, and vowel length, since these features change the meaning of words in English.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students practise the minimal pair 'ship' and 'sheep', noting that the short vowel /ɪ/ in 'ship' differs from the long vowel /iː/ in 'sheep', and that mispronouncing one changes the meaning of the word.
sla_notes_daily_life: Clear pronunciation helps learners communicate confidently and be understood correctly in conversations, interviews and presentations.
sla_exercise: Give one pair of words that sound almost the same but have different meanings.::Any correct minimal pair, e.g. 'ship/sheep' or 'cat/cut'.||Why is word stress important in English pronunciation?::Because placing stress on the wrong syllable can change the meaning or make a word hard to understand.||What technique can a learner use to practise difficult sounds?::Repeating tongue twisters or words after a model speaker (drilling).

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to write new vocabulary from conversations and written texts on particular topics, expanding their word bank for both oral and written communication.
sla_notes_details: Students identify new words from texts or conversations, work out their meanings from context, record them with definitions and example sentences, and use them actively in speaking and writing. Word-formation techniques such as adding prefixes and suffixes, and relationships such as synonyms and antonyms, are used to deepen understanding.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, from the word 'kind', students form the antonym 'unkind' by adding the prefix 'un-', and the adverb 'kindly' by adding the suffix '-ly', then use each new word in a sentence.
sla_notes_daily_life: A wide vocabulary helps learners express themselves precisely when writing letters, telling stories, or discussing topics such as sports, tourism or agriculture.

sla_notes_details: Students study the target grammatical structure through examples, identify how it is formed, and practise it by constructing their own sentences orally and in writing. sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson develops students' ability to sequence the order of events in stories by engaging closely with written texts.
sla_notes_details: Students read a passage silently or aloud, identify key information such as main ideas, sequence of events, facts versus opinions, or the writer's intended meaning, and then respond to comprehension questions orally or in writing. Strategies such as skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, and using context clues to infer meaning are practised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after reading a short story, students list the events in the order they happened using sequence words such as 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally', before writing a short summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reading skills help learners understand newspapers, notices, textbooks and other texts they meet outside the classroom.
sla_exercise: Name two sequence words used to show the order of events in a story.::Any two of: first, then, after that, finally, next.||What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?::A fact can be proven true, while an opinion is a personal belief or judgement.||Explain one strategy for finding the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a text.::Using context clues, such as the surrounding words, to guess the meaning.

sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to paraphrase various oral messages from different contexts accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to paraphrase various oral messages from different contexts after listening to spoken texts such as presentations, stories or recordings. Strong listening comprehension is the foundation for accurate spoken and written responses.
sla_notes_details: Students listen attentively to an oral text (a presentation, recording, or teacher narration), note down key words and ideas, and then use these notes to respond, summarise or paraphrase what they heard. Emphasis is placed on listening for gist first, then for specific details, before producing an accurate spoken or written response.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after listening to a short recorded story about a market day, students identify who the characters are, what happened first, next and last, and then retell the story in their own words to a partner.
sla_notes_daily_life: This skill helps learners follow announcements, instructions and conversations correctly in everyday situations such as at school, at home or on the radio.
sla_exercise: What should a listener do before trying to answer questions about a spoken text?::Listen attentively for the overall meaning (gist) before focusing on specific details.||Why is note-taking useful while listening?::It helps the listener remember key ideas to use when responding or summarising.||State one way to check that you understood a spoken message correctly.::Restate or paraphrase the message back to the speaker to confirm understanding.

sla_name: Communication skills: Express ideas and opinions in different interpersonal communication
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to express ideas and opinions in different interpersonal communication settings accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to express ideas and opinions in different interpersonal communication settings, developing skills for effective interpersonal and group communication.
sla_notes_details: Students study appropriate language, tone and non-verbal cues (such as eye contact, gestures and facial expression) used in different communicative settings. Through role play, dialogue and discussion, they practise expressing and responding to ideas politely and appropriately depending on the audience and context.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a role play, one student greets an elder formally using 'Good morning, how are you today?' while greeting a peer informally using 'Hey, what's up?', showing how register changes with audience.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills help learners communicate respectfully and effectively with different people in daily life, such as teachers, family members, and the wider community.
sla_exercise: Give one example of a non-verbal cue used in communication.::Any correct example, e.g. eye contact, a nod, or a gesture.||Why should language change depending on who you are speaking to?::Because different audiences (e.g. elders versus peers) expect different levels of formality and respect.||Give one polite expression used to express an opinion.::Any correct example, e.g. 'In my opinion...' or 'I think that...'.

sla_name: Using grammar: Express daily routines
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to express daily routines accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson enables students to express daily routines, applying grammatical structures accurately in a specific context.
sla_notes_details: Students study the target structure through examples relevant to the context, then practise producing their own oral and written sentences describing real situations. The teacher guides students to notice how the structure changes meaning (for example between ongoing and habitual actions) and corrects common errors.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to express daily routines a student says 'I wake up at six o'clock and go to school', while to express an ongoing action the same student says 'I am going to school now', showing the contrast between simple and progressive forms.
sla_notes_daily_life: Learners use these structures every day to describe their routines, locations, feelings and needs when talking with family, friends and in the community.
sla_exercise: Complete the sentence using the correct tense: 'Every morning, she ___ (walk) to school.'::walks||Rewrite the sentence to show an action happening now: 'He plays football.'::He is playing football.||Give one example sentence describing your own daily routine.::Any grammatically correct sentence describing a routine, e.g. 'I brush my teeth every morning.'

sla_notes_intro: This lesson guides students to recognise the main stages of writing texts, developing their ability to write for a specific purpose and audience.
sla_notes_details: Students study a model text to identify its structure, tone and typical vocabulary, then plan and write their own text following the same conventions. Emphasis is placed on the appropriate greeting or opening, logical organisation of ideas, and a suitable closing, matched to the purpose of the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when writing a friendly letter, a student begins with 'Dear Aunt Mary,', writes the body in a warm, personal tone, and closes with 'Your loving nephew,' followed by their name.
sla_notes_daily_life: These writing skills are used whenever learners need to communicate in writing outside the classroom, such as writing to relatives, applying for opportunities, or sharing news.
sla_exercise: Name one part that every letter should include.::Any correct part, e.g. a greeting/salutation, the body, or a closing.||Give an appropriate opening greeting for a letter to a family member.::Any correct example, e.g. 'Dear Mother,' or 'Dear Uncle,'.||Why is it important to plan a piece of writing before starting?::Planning helps organise ideas logically so the final text is clear and well structured.

sla_name: Listening task: Participate in various conversations in different communicative settings
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to participate in various conversations in different communicative settings accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to participate in various conversations in different communicative settings after listening to spoken texts such as presentations, stories or recordings. Strong listening comprehension is the foundation for accurate spoken and written responses.
sla_notes_details: Students listen attentively to an oral text (a presentation, recording, or teacher narration), note down key words and ideas, and then use these notes to respond, summarise or paraphrase what they heard. Emphasis is placed on listening for gist first, then for specific details, before producing an accurate spoken or written response.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after listening to a short recorded story about a market day, students identify who the characters are, what happened first, next and last, and then retell the story in their own words to a partner.
sla_notes_daily_life: This skill helps learners follow announcements, instructions and conversations correctly in everyday situations such as at school, at home or on the radio.
sla_exercise: What should a listener do before trying to answer questions about a spoken text?::Listen attentively for the overall meaning (gist) before focusing on specific details.||Why is note-taking useful while listening?::It helps the listener remember key ideas to use when responding or summarising.||State one way to check that you understood a spoken message correctly.::Restate or paraphrase the message back to the speaker to confirm understanding.

sla_teaching_aids: Mirror for articulation practice|Audio recordings|Word cards
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson focuses on helping students to construct sentences with proper intonation, building intelligible pronunciation and fluency in spoken English.
sla_notes_details: Students listen to a model (teacher or recording) pronouncing target words or sounds correctly, then practise through repetition, tongue twisters, games or dictation. Attention is paid to sound distinctions (minimal pairs), word stress, and vowel length, since these features change the meaning of words in English.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students practise the minimal pair 'ship' and 'sheep', noting that the short vowel /ɪ/ in 'ship' differs from the long vowel /iː/ in 'sheep', and that mispronouncing one changes the meaning of the word.
sla_notes_daily_life: Clear pronunciation helps learners communicate confidently and be understood correctly in conversations, interviews and presentations.
sla_exercise: Give one pair of words that sound almost the same but have different meanings.::Any correct minimal pair, e.g. 'ship/sheep' or 'cat/cut'.||Why is word stress important in English pronunciation?::Because placing stress on the wrong syllable can change the meaning or make a word hard to understand.||What technique can a learner use to practise difficult sounds?::Repeating tongue twisters or words after a model speaker (drilling).

sla_notes_intro: This lesson guides students to use cohesive devices to deliver oral presentations of events, using correct grammatical structures and appropriate vocabulary.
sla_notes_details: Students study the target grammatical structure through examples, identify how it is formed, and practise it by constructing their own sentences orally and in writing. Feedback from peers and the teacher helps students correct errors in tense, agreement, word order and vocabulary choice.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when practising past and present tense forms, a student changes 'She writes a letter every day' (present) to 'She wrote a letter yesterday' (past), noting the change in the verb form.
sla_notes_daily_life: Accurate grammar allows learners to be clearly understood when narrating events, debating issues or writing formal and informal texts.

sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to recognise words with opposite meanings from conversations and written texts, expanding their word bank for both oral and written communication.
sla_notes_details: Students identify new words from texts or conversations, work out their meanings from context, record them with definitions and example sentences, and use them actively in speaking and writing. Word-formation techniques such as adding prefixes and suffixes, and relationships such as synonyms and antonyms, are used to deepen understanding.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, from the word 'kind', students form the antonym 'unkind' by adding the prefix 'un-', and the adverb 'kindly' by adding the suffix '-ly', then use each new word in a sentence.
sla_notes_daily_life: A wide vocabulary helps learners express themselves precisely when writing letters, telling stories, or discussing topics such as sports, tourism or agriculture.
sla_exercise: Form the opposite of the word 'kind' by adding a prefix.::Unkind.||Change the adjective 'slow' into an adverb.::Slowly.||Use the word 'agriculture' in a sentence of your own.::Any grammatically correct sentence using 'agriculture' correctly.

learning_activity_name: Express the main ideas from a text
sla_name: Reading comprehension: Express the main ideas from a text
sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to express the main ideas from a text accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson develops students' ability to express the main ideas from a text by engaging closely with written texts.
sla_notes_details: Students read a passage silently or aloud, identify key information such as main ideas, sequence of events, facts versus opinions, or the writer's intended meaning, and then respond to comprehension questions orally or in writing. Strategies such as skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, and using context clues to infer meaning are practised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after reading a short story, students list the events in the order they happened using sequence words such as 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally', before writing a short summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reading skills help learners understand newspapers, notices, textbooks and other texts they meet outside the classroom.
sla_exercise: Name two sequence words used to show the order of events in a story.::Any two of: first, then, after that, finally, next.||What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?::A fact can be proven true, while an opinion is a personal belief or judgement.||Explain one strategy for finding the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a text.::Using context clues, such as the surrounding words, to guess the meaning.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to express ideas and opinions in different group communicative settings, developing skills for effective interpersonal and group communication.
sla_notes_details: Students study appropriate language, tone and non-verbal cues (such as eye contact, gestures and facial expression) used in different communicative settings. Through role play, dialogue and discussion, they practise expressing and responding to ideas politely and appropriately depending on the audience and context.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a role play, one student greets an elder formally using 'Good morning, how are you today?' while greeting a peer informally using 'Hey, what's up?', showing how register changes with audience.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills help learners communicate respectfully and effectively with different people in daily life, such as teachers, family members, and the wider community.
sla_exercise: Give one example of a non-verbal cue used in communication.::Any correct example, e.g. eye contact, a nod, or a gesture.||Why should language change depending on who you are speaking to?::Because different audiences (e.g. elders versus peers) expect different levels of formality and respect.||Give one polite expression used to express an opinion.::Any correct example, e.g. 'In my opinion...' or 'I think that...'.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson enables students to describe various locations, applying grammatical structures accurately in a specific context.
sla_notes_details: Students study the target structure through examples relevant to the context, then practise producing their own oral and written sentences describing real situations. sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to express daily routines a student says 'I wake up at six o'clock and go to school', while to express an ongoing action the same student says 'I am going to school now', showing the contrast between simple and progressive forms.
sla_notes_daily_life: Learners use these structures every day to describe their routines, locations, feelings and needs when talking with family, friends and in the community.

sla_notes_details: Students study a model text to identify its structure, tone and typical vocabulary, then plan and write their own text following the same conventions. sla_assessment_criteria: Students are able to distinguish facts from opinions within a given text accurately and confidently.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson develops students' ability to distinguish facts from opinions within a given text by engaging closely with written texts.
sla_notes_details: Students read a passage silently or aloud, identify key information such as main ideas, sequence of events, facts versus opinions, or the writer's intended meaning, and then respond to comprehension questions orally or in writing. Strategies such as skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, and using context clues to infer meaning are practised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after reading a short story, students list the events in the order they happened using sequence words such as 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally', before writing a short summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reading skills help learners understand newspapers, notices, textbooks and other texts they meet outside the classroom.
sla_exercise: Name two sequence words used to show the order of events in a story.::Any two of: first, then, after that, finally, next.||What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?::A fact can be proven true, while an opinion is a personal belief or judgement.||Explain one strategy for finding the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a text.::Using context clues, such as the surrounding words, to guess the meaning.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to discuss information from various oral sources after listening to spoken texts such as presentations, stories or recordings. Strong listening comprehension is the foundation for accurate spoken and written responses.
sla_notes_details: Students listen attentively to an oral text (a presentation, recording, or teacher narration), note down key words and ideas, and then use these notes to respond, summarise or paraphrase what they heard. Emphasis is placed on listening for gist first, then for specific details, before producing an accurate spoken or written response.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson develops students' ability to compare ideas from various texts by engaging closely with written texts.
sla_notes_details: Students read a passage silently or aloud, identify key information such as main ideas, sequence of events, facts versus opinions, or the writer's intended meaning, and then respond to comprehension questions orally or in writing. Strategies such as skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, and using context clues to infer meaning are practised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after reading a short story, students list the events in the order they happened using sequence words such as 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally', before writing a short summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reading skills help learners understand newspapers, notices, textbooks and other texts they meet outside the classroom.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to explain the concept of interpretation, applying the basic principles of oral interpretation between English and Kiswahili.
sla_notes_details: Students learn that interpretation means conveying a spoken message from a source language into a target language accurately and immediately, while keeping the original meaning, tone and intent. They practise both consecutive interpretation (interpreting after the speaker pauses) and simple simultaneous interpretation in short, familiar contexts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a speaker says in English 'Welcome to our school, please take your seats,' the student interprets it into Kiswahili as 'Karibuni shuleni kwetu, tafadhali kaeni,' keeping the same meaning and tone.
sla_notes_daily_life: Interpretation skills help learners assist communication between English and Kiswahili speakers at school, in church or mosque gatherings, and in community meetings.
sla_exercise: What is the main goal of interpretation?::To convey a spoken message accurately from one language into another while keeping its meaning.||Name the two types of interpretation practised in this lesson.::Consecutive interpretation and simultaneous interpretation.||Interpret this greeting into Kiswahili: 'Good morning, how are you?'::Habari za asubuhi, hujambo? (or an equivalent correct Kiswahili greeting).

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to explain the concept of translation, applying the basic principles of written translation between English and Kiswahili.
sla_notes_details: Students learn that translation involves changing a written text from a source language into a target language while preserving its meaning, register and purpose. They study communicative translation techniques, which prioritise natural, meaningful expression over word-for-word conversion, and practise translating short texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the English notice 'No entry without permission' is translated communicatively into Kiswahili as 'Hairuhusiwi kuingia bila kibali,' rather than a stiff word-for-word version.
sla_notes_daily_life: Translation skills allow learners to make information such as notices, timetables and short documents accessible to both English and Kiswahili speakers in their community.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between translation and interpretation?::Translation deals with written text, while interpretation deals with spoken language.||Translate the phrase 'Welcome to our school' into Kiswahili.::Karibu shuleni kwetu (or an equivalent correct translation).||Why should a translator avoid strict word-for-word translation?::Because it can produce unnatural or unclear meaning; communicative translation preserves the intended meaning better.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson guides students to assess the language used in selected poems and plays, developing an appreciation of literary language and its aesthetic value.
sla_notes_details: Students read a selected literary text closely, identifying stylistic features such as imagery, figurative language, rhythm and word choice, and discuss how these features create meaning and emotional effect. They also reflect on their own values and compare them with those expressed in the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a poem describing rain as 'tears of the sky', students discuss how this metaphor creates a sad, reflective mood and compare it with their own feelings about rain.
sla_notes_daily_life: Appreciating literature helps learners understand different perspectives on life and express their own feelings and values more creatively.
sla_exercise: What is a metaphor?::A figure of speech that describes something by referring to it as if it were something else, without using 'like' or 'as'.||Give one example of figurative language.::Any correct example, e.g. metaphor, simile, or personification.||Why is it useful to compare your own values with those expressed in a literary text?::It helps deepen understanding of the text and reflect critically on one's own perspective.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to describe different genres of written literature and their conventions, building analytical skills for studying different types of literature.
sla_notes_details: Students identify features that distinguish literary genres such as poetry, prose and drama, and learn the criteria used to critique a literary work, including its form (structure, language) and content (theme, message). They apply these criteria to analyse and critique selected texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students compare a poem and a play on the same theme of friendship, noting that the poem uses condensed, rhythmic language while the play uses dialogue and stage directions to develop the same theme.
sla_notes_daily_life: Genre analysis skills help learners choose and enjoy appropriate reading materials and express informed opinions about books, films and plays they encounter.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to analyse techniques of critiquing poems and plays based on their conventions, building analytical skills for studying different types of literature.
sla_notes_details: Students identify features that distinguish literary genres such as poetry, prose and drama, and learn the criteria used to critique a literary work, including its form (structure, language) and content (theme, message). They apply these criteria to analyse and critique selected texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students compare a poem and a play on the same theme of friendship, noting that the poem uses condensed, rhythmic language while the play uses dialogue and stage directions to develop the same theme.
sla_notes_daily_life: Genre analysis skills help learners choose and enjoy appropriate reading materials and express informed opinions about books, films and plays they encounter.
sla_exercise: Name the three main genres of literature.::Poetry, prose, and drama.||What does 'form' refer to when critiquing a literary work?::The structure and language techniques used in the work, such as rhyme, rhythm or dialogue.||Give one difference between poetry and drama.::Poetry is typically written in condensed, rhythmic lines, while drama is written mainly as dialogue meant to be performed.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson develops students' ability to discuss the author's motives in a given text by engaging closely with written texts.
sla_notes_details: Students read a passage silently or aloud, identify key information such as main ideas, sequence of events, facts versus opinions, or the writer's intended meaning, and then respond to comprehension questions orally or in writing. Strategies such as skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, and using context clues to infer meaning are practised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after reading a short story, students list the events in the order they happened using sequence words such as 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally', before writing a short summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reading skills help learners understand newspapers, notices, textbooks and other texts they meet outside the classroom.
sla_exercise: Name two sequence words used to show the order of events in a story.::Any two of: first, then, after that, finally, next.||What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?::A fact can be proven true, while an opinion is a personal belief or judgement.||Explain one strategy for finding the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a text.::Using context clues, such as the surrounding words, to guess the meaning.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to deduce the main ideas from an oral presentation or language task after listening to spoken texts such as presentations, stories or recordings. Strong listening comprehension is the foundation for accurate spoken and written responses.
sla_notes_details: Students listen attentively to an oral text (a presentation, recording, or teacher narration), note down key words and ideas, and then use these notes to respond, summarise or paraphrase what they heard. Emphasis is placed on listening for gist first, then for specific details, before producing an accurate spoken or written response.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after listening to a short recorded story about a market day, students identify who the characters are, what happened first, next and last, and then retell the story in their own words to a partner.
sla_notes_daily_life: This skill helps learners follow announcements, instructions and conversations correctly in everyday situations such as at school, at home or on the radio.
sla_exercise: What should a listener do before trying to answer questions about a spoken text?::Listen attentively for the overall meaning (gist) before focusing on specific details.||Why is note-taking useful while listening?::It helps the listener remember key ideas to use when responding or summarising.||State one way to check that you understood a spoken message correctly.::Restate or paraphrase the message back to the speaker to confirm understanding.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to analyse different functional texts in terms of purpose, content, organisation, format and design, developing awareness of how everyday functional texts are structured and used.
sla_notes_details: Students examine functional texts such as recipes, product manuals, transport schedules, forms, brochures and menus, identifying their purpose, organisation, format and typical language. sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students examine a bus transport schedule, noting how times and destinations are organised in a table for quick reference, then design their own simple schedule for a school event.

sla_exercise: Name two examples of functional texts.::Any two of: recipes, product manuals, transport schedules, forms, brochures, menus.||Why is format important in a functional text such as a schedule?::A clear format, such as a table, allows readers to find information quickly and accurately.||What should be considered when composing a functional text?::Its purpose, its intended audience, and using a format that presents information clearly.

sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to interpret messages in informal contexts, applying the basic principles of oral interpretation between English and Kiswahili.
sla_notes_details: Students learn that interpretation means conveying a spoken message from a source language into a target language accurately and immediately, while keeping the original meaning, tone and intent. They practise both consecutive interpretation (interpreting after the speaker pauses) and simple simultaneous interpretation in short, familiar contexts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a speaker says in English 'Welcome to our school, please take your seats,' the student interprets it into Kiswahili as 'Karibuni shuleni kwetu, tafadhali kaeni,' keeping the same meaning and tone.
sla_notes_daily_life: Interpretation skills help learners assist communication between English and Kiswahili speakers at school, in church or mosque gatherings, and in community meetings.
sla_exercise: What is the main goal of interpretation?::To convey a spoken message accurately from one language into another while keeping its meaning.||Name the two types of interpretation practised in this lesson.::Consecutive interpretation and simultaneous interpretation.||Interpret this greeting into Kiswahili: 'Good morning, how are you?'::Habari za asubuhi, hujambo? (or an equivalent correct Kiswahili greeting).

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to translate texts in contexts outside the school, applying the basic principles of written translation between English and Kiswahili.
sla_notes_details: Students learn that translation involves changing a written text from a source language into a target language while preserving its meaning, register and purpose. They study communicative translation techniques, which prioritise natural, meaningful expression over word-for-word conversion, and practise translating short texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the English notice 'No entry without permission' is translated communicatively into Kiswahili as 'Hairuhusiwi kuingia bila kibali,' rather than a stiff word-for-word version.
sla_notes_daily_life: Translation skills allow learners to make information such as notices, timetables and short documents accessible to both English and Kiswahili speakers in their community.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between translation and interpretation?::Translation deals with written text, while interpretation deals with spoken language.||Translate the phrase 'Welcome to our school' into Kiswahili.::Karibu shuleni kwetu (or an equivalent correct translation).||Why should a translator avoid strict word-for-word translation?::Because it can produce unnatural or unclear meaning; communicative translation preserves the intended meaning better.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to examine the socio-political and cultural issues portrayed in a selected novella, understanding the background against which a literary text was produced.
sla_notes_details: Students investigate the socio-political, economic and cultural setting in which a literary text was written, and consider how that setting shapes its themes and message. They then relate the issues raised in the text to real experiences in their own community.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson helps students to analyse techniques of critiquing literary texts based on their conventions, building analytical skills for studying different types of literature.
sla_notes_details: Students identify features that distinguish literary genres such as poetry, prose and drama, and learn the criteria used to critique a literary work, including its form (structure, language) and content (theme, message). They apply these criteria to analyse and critique selected texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students compare a poem and a play on the same theme of friendship, noting that the poem uses condensed, rhythmic language while the play uses dialogue and stage directions to develop the same theme.
sla_notes_daily_life: Genre analysis skills help learners choose and enjoy appropriate reading materials and express informed opinions about books, films and plays they encounter.
sla_exercise: Name the three main genres of literature.::Poetry, prose, and drama.||What does 'form' refer to when critiquing a literary work?::The structure and language techniques used in the work, such as rhyme, rhythm or dialogue.||Give one difference between poetry and drama.::Poetry is typically written in condensed, rhythmic lines, while drama is written mainly as dialogue meant to be performed.

sla_notes_intro: This lesson guides students to apply literary skills to compose short stories on various topics, developing their own skills as creative writers of literature.
sla_notes_details: Students learn the steps of composing an original literary work, from choosing a topic and generating ideas, to drafting, revising and finalising the piece using appropriate literary language and devices. Where relevant, they also learn appropriate platforms for sharing or publishing their finished work.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student drafts a free verse poem about friendship, revises it to include a simile such as 'friendship is like a warm fire on a cold night', and then shares the final version with classmates.
sla_notes_daily_life: Creative writing allows learners to express their own experiences and feelings, and to share their work with a wider audience through school note boards or online platforms.
